materials, blood and IV fluid for transfusion will 
be stocked. The hospital casualty room is to 
be equipped with resuscitation equipment like 
suction apparatus, airways laryngoscope, pulse 
oxymeter, defibrillator and life saving drugs. In the 
aftermath of a flood, public health response is one 
of the prime responsibilities of medical authorities. 
They will ensure safe water supply and clean food 
availability along with maintenance of hygiene and 
sanitation by proper bio-waste disposal. Water 
testing and food inspection is required to be carried 
out regularly to prevent outbreak of any epidemic. 
An effective communication system is an essential 
requirement for prompt medical response.

131
• When re-entering buildings or homes,
use extreme caution.
Tsunami-driven floodwater may have
damaged buildings where you least
expect it.   Carefully watch every step
you take.
• Wear long pants, a long-sleeved shirt,
and sturdy shoes.
The most common injury following a
disaster is cut feet.
• Use battery-powered lanterns or
flashlights when examining buildings.
Battery-powered lighting is the safest
and easiest to use, and it does not
present a fire hazard for the user,
occupants, or building. DO NOT USE
CANDLES.
• Examine walls, floors, doors,
staircases, and windows to make sure
that the building is not in danger of
collapsing.
• Inspect foundations for cracks or other
damage.
Cracks and damage to a foundation
can render a building uninhabitable.
• Look for fire hazards.
Under the earthquake action there
may be broken or leaking gas lines, and
under the tsunami flooded electrical
circuits, or submerged furnaces or
electrical appliances. Flammable or
explosive materials may have come
from upstream. Fire is the most
frequent hazard following floods.
• Check for gas leaks.
If you smell gas or hear a blowing or
hissing noise, open a window and get
everyone outside quickly. Turn off the
gas using the outside main valve if you
can, and call the gas company from a
neighbour's home. If you turn off the
gas for any reason, it must be turned
back on by a professional.
• Look for electrical system damage.
If you see sparks or broken or frayed
wires, or if you smell burning
insulation, turn off the electricity at the
main fuse box or circuit breaker. If you
have to step in water to get to the fuse
box or circuit breaker, call an electrician
first for advice. Electrical equipment
should be checked and dried before
being returned to service.
• Check for damage to sewage and
water lines.
If you suspect sewage lines are
damaged under the quake, avoid using
the toilets and call a plumber. If water
pipes are damaged, contact the water
company and avoid using water from
the tap. You can obtain safe water from
undamaged water heaters or by
melting ice cubes that were made
before the tsunami hit.

41
Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.
Schedule for Response Activities
8.11.1  All the response activities outlined above
require detailed planning and comprehensive
mobilisation of manpower. The schedule given in
Table 10 (Pg 42) is considered reasonable at this
juncture; all activities will be institutionalised by and
continued beyond December 2008.

Prepare and dispatch a medical kit containing IV fluids, analgesics/antipyretics, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics or throat lozenges as per local protocol for severe sore throat with dehydration risk.
Include basic airway adjuncts (suction apparatus, laryngoscope) and life‑saving drugs in case of respiratory compromise.
Ensure the receiving medical facility has stocked tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, and anti‑diarrhoea drugs as listed for flood‑related medical stores.

7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

• When re-entering buildings or homes,
use extreme caution.
Tsunami-driven floodwater may have
damaged buildings where you least
expect it.   Carefully watch every step
you take.
• Wear long pants, a long-sleeved shirt,
and sturdy shoes.
The most common injury following a
disaster is cut feet.
• Use battery-powered lanterns or
flashlights when examining buildings.
Battery-powered lighting is the safest
and easiest to use, and it does not
present a fire hazard for the user,
occupants, or building. DO NOT USE
CANDLES.
• Examine walls, floors, doors,
staircases, and windows to make sure
that the building is not in danger of
collapsing.
• Inspect foundations for cracks or other
damage.
Cracks and damage to a foundation
can render a building uninhabitable.
• Look for fire hazards.
Under the earthquake action there
may be broken or leaking gas lines, and
under the tsunami flooded electrical
circuits, or submerged furnaces or
electrical appliances. Flammable or
explosive materials may have come
from upstream. Fire is the most
frequent hazard following floods.
• Check for gas leaks.
If you smell gas or hear a blowing or
hissing noise, open a window and get
everyone outside quickly. Turn off the
gas using the outside main valve if you
can, and call the gas company from a
neighbour's home. If you turn off the
gas for any reason, it must be turned
back on by a professional.
• Look for electrical system damage.
If you see sparks or broken or frayed
wires, or if you smell burning
insulation, turn off the electricity at the
main fuse box or circuit breaker. If you
have to step in water to get to the fuse
box or circuit breaker, call an electrician
first for advice. Electrical equipment
should be checked and dried before
being returned to service.
• Check for damage to sewage and
water lines.
If you suspect sewage lines are
damaged under the quake, avoid using
the toilets and call a plumber. If water
pipes are damaged, contact the water
company and avoid using water from
the tap. You can obtain safe water from
undamaged water heaters or by
melting ice cubes that were made
before the tsunami hit.

7.6 Medical Preparedness and 
Response
7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

• When re-entering buildings or homes,
use extreme caution.
Tsunami-driven floodwater may have
damaged buildings where you least
expect it.   Carefully watch every step
you take.
• Wear long pants, a long-sleeved shirt,
and sturdy shoes.
The most common injury following a
disaster is cut feet.
• Use battery-powered lanterns or
flashlights when examining buildings.
Battery-powered lighting is the safest
and easiest to use, and it does not
present a fire hazard for the user,
occupants, or building. DO NOT USE
CANDLES.
• Examine walls, floors, doors,
staircases, and windows to make sure
that the building is not in danger of
collapsing.
• Inspect foundations for cracks or other
damage.
Cracks and damage to a foundation
can render a building uninhabitable.
• Look for fire hazards.
Under the earthquake action there
may be broken or leaking gas lines, and
under the tsunami flooded electrical
circuits, or submerged furnaces or
electrical appliances. Flammable or
explosive materials may have come
from upstream. Fire is the most
frequent hazard following floods.
• Check for gas leaks.
If you smell gas or hear a blowing or
hissing noise, open a window and get
everyone outside quickly. Turn off the
gas using the outside main valve if you
can, and call the gas company from a
neighbour's home. If you turn off the
gas for any reason, it must be turned
back on by a professional.
• Look for electrical system damage.
If you see sparks or broken or frayed
wires, or if you smell burning
insulation, turn off the electricity at the
main fuse box or circuit breaker. If you
have to step in water to get to the fuse
box or circuit breaker, call an electrician
first for advice. Electrical equipment
should be checked and dried before
being returned to service.
• Check for damage to sewage and
water lines.
If you suspect sewage lines are
damaged under the quake, avoid using
the toilets and call a plumber. If water
pipes are damaged, contact the water
company and avoid using water from
the tap. You can obtain safe water from
undamaged water heaters or by
melting ice cubes that were made
before the tsunami hit.

Deploy mobile field hospitals or ARMVs (Advanced Rescue Medical Vehicles) to provide immediate care.
If transport time is long, request heli‑ambulance support for rapid evacuation to a hospital.
Provide basic airway management, dressing materials, splints, and portable X‑ray as needed.
Conduct triage, initiate resuscitation if required, and arrange medical evacuation to a definitive care facility.
Prepare a medical kit containing intravenous (IV) fluid, oxygen supply, and basic dressing materials.
Include antibiotics, anti‑diarrhoea drugs, and tetanus toxoid as part of the kit.
Ensure availability of ventilators or basic airway adjuncts if respiratory compromise is suspected.
Coordinate with identified large‑scale medical stores to procure the listed items promptly.
Deliver the assembled kit to the location where the patient is being treated.

final_json.report: The caller reports a severe sore throat with difficulty drinking and eating. Retrieved documents focus on medical preparedness for flood disasters, outlining emergency medical response teams, mobile field hospitals, and required medical supplies. Based on this evidence, medical_help resources should be mobilized using QRMTs, ARMVs, and heli‑ambulance support, and medical_products should include IV fluids, antibiotics, and supportive care items. No specific guidance for sore‑throat treatment is present in the sources, indicating an evidence gap for targeted therapy, but the general emergency response framework can be applied to provide immediate care and evacuation if needed.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

require detailed planning and comprehensive
mobilisation of manpower. The schedule given in

final_json.scenario: Food and medical facilities required urgently at Qadirpur (Ghotki)

instructions: Activate existing MoUs with approved food suppliers to procure family packs of essential food provisions.
Coordinate with central/state ministries to arrange delivery of infant and small‑child nutrition supplies.
Utilize FCI storage facilities to stage grain and cooked food stocks for rapid distribution to Qadirpur.
Deploy distribution teams to deliver safe water and clean food to affected populations, following public health guidelines.
Mobilize QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, ARMVs and heli‑ambulances to Qadirpur immediately.
Equip deployed units with dressing material, splints, portable X‑ray machines, mobile operation theatres, resuscitation equipment and life‑saving drugs.
Conduct on‑site triage, resuscitation and medical evacuation of victims requiring hospitalisation according to SOPs.
Prepare medical kits containing IV fluid, ventilators, oxygen, dressing materials, tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, vaccines, anti‑snake venom and anti‑diarrhoea drugs.
Identify and activate large‑scale medical stores to procure the listed items.
Stock hospital casualty rooms with resuscitation equipment (suction apparatus, airways, laryngoscope, pulse oximeter, defibrillator) and life‑saving drugs.
Ensure trained medical and paramedical staff are available to manage flood casualties.

final_json.report: Urgent response initiated for Qadirpur (Ghotki) following flood impact. Food provisions will be sourced via existing MoUs and FCI stocks, ensuring safe water and clean food distribution. Emergency medical help will be delivered through QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, ARMVs and heli‑ambulances with full complement of trauma and evacuation equipment. Medical products—including IV fluids, ventilators, antibiotics and other essential drugs—will be assembled into kits and stocked in casualty rooms, supported by identified large‑scale medical stores and trained staff. All actions are based on documented protocols from the retrieved sources; no evidence gaps were identified.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical

operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise

equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an

provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and

supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas

resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.

victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a

(NYKS) will provide support services to the response
teams at the local level under the overall guidance
and supervision of the local administration.
Emergency Relief
8.3.1  Trained community level teams will assist
in planning and setting up emergency shelters,
distributing relief among the affected people,
identifying missing people, and addressing the
needs of education, health care, water supply and
sanitation, food etc., of the affected community.
Members of these teams will be made aware of
the specific requirements of the disaster affected
communities. These teams will also assist the
government in identifying the most vulnerable
people who may need special assistance following
an earthquake.
Incident Command System (ICS)
8.4.1  All response activities will be undertaken at
the local level through a suitably devised ICS
coordinated by the local administration through the
EOC.  State governments will commission and
maintain EOCs at appropriate levels for the
coordination of human resources, relief supplies and
equipment. SOPs for the EOCs will be developed
by state governments and integrated within the
framework of the ICS, which will take advantage of
modern technologies and tools, such as GIS maps,
scenarios and simulation models for effectively
responding to disasters. GIS maps available from
other sources, such as the city planning
departments will be compiled considering their
potential application after a disaster. The state
governments/SDMAs will undertake the training of
personnel involved in the ICS.
Community Based Disaster Response
8.5.1  A number of organisations, like NGOs, self-
help groups, CBOs, youth organisations, women’s
groups, volunteer agencies, Civil Defence, Home
Guards, etc. normally volunteer their services in the
aftermath of any disaster. State government/SDMAs
and DDMAs will coordinate the allocation of these
human resources for performing various response
activities. State governments will work with these
agencies to understand and plan their roles in the
command chain of the ICS, and incorporate them
in the DM plans.

Earthquake Response
8.1.1  The management and control of the adverse
consequences of future earthquakes will require
coordinated, prompt and effective response
systems at the central and state government levels,
especially at the district and the community levels.
Many of the components of response initiatives are
the same for different types of disasters and
systems need to be developed considering the
multi-hazard scenario of various regions in order to
optimally utilise available resources.
8.1.2   For earthquakes, depending on their
magnitude, the scale of response and the
corresponding role players will be identified and
mobilised at the district, state or national levels.
Systems will be institutionalised by the DMAs, at
various levels, for coordination between the various
agencies like central government ministries and
departments, state governments, district
administration, ULBs, PRIs and other stakeholders
for effective post-earthquake response.
8.1.3  The severity of an earthquake is often
underestimated, immediately after its occurrence.
The preliminary assessment of severity of the
earthquake is based on its magnitude and depth
collected from online seismological instruments.
Field observation data, once available, will be used
to make an accurate assessment. Immediately
following the occurrence of an earthquake, the IMD
will disseminate the details of its magnitude and
epicentre to all agencies concerned.  This will help
the state governments to undertake their response
appropriately.

specialised search and rescue teams. Thus, trained
and equipped teams consisting of local people will

Flood Response
An effective and prompt response to floods 
is very important for minimising the loss of lives 
and properties and providing immediate relief 
to the affected people. The role of communities 
and NGOs is vital in search, rescue and relief 
operations. Immediate medical assistance to 
the affected people and steps for prevention of 
outbreak of epidemics after the floods are essential 
components of flood response. As per provisions of 
the DM Act, 2005, the GOI has constituted National 
Disaster Response Force (NDRF) for the purpose of 
specialised response to disasters. Over and above 
this, a mechanism for coordinated approach and 
efforts are required for effective response. All these 
aspects have been covered in the eighth chapter 
titled ‘Flood Response’.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

final_json.report: A family of 15 whose home has collapsed requires emergency assistance. The incident context and need for emergency relief are supported by national disaster management guidelines (ndmaguidelinesmanagementofsunamis.pdf p.94; a.pdf p.61). Shelter, medical help, medical products, and search and rescue have sufficient documented procedures and were therefore dispatched with concrete actions. No specific actionable guidance was found in the retrieved documents for water, food, clothing, money, or tools, indicating evidence gaps for these resources. Immediate deployment of shelter supplies, medical response teams, medical kits, and SAR teams is recommended while additional sourcing for the missing resources should be pursued.

instructions: Identify shelter suppliers capable of providing tents or temporary shelters up to the village level and activate pre‑existing MoUs for rapid supply (within 24 hours).

All required resources have sufficient evidential support; no evidence gaps were identified.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

final_json.report: The incident reported in SCEN-AGR-02 indicates an urgent humanitarian crisis with immediate needs for water, food, and medical assistance. Query sources outline general disaster response goals. Food assistance can be mobilized using existing supplier MoUs, infant/child provisions, and FCI grain storage as detailed in ndmp-2019.pdf p.312 and reinforced by flood response guidance (floods.pdf p.67). Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical

8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be

Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by

equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical

instructions: Activate water supply agencies to provide safe drinking water to the affected population.
Distribute water purification tablets and set up temporary water treatment points as per public health response guidelines.
Mobilize food distribution teams to deliver clean, ready‑to‑eat food parcels.
Coordinate with suppliers under existing MOUs to ensure rapid delivery of essential food provisions, including infant and child nutrition packs.
Identify and activate shelter suppliers to provide tents, tarpaulins and temporary shelter materials.
Deploy pre‑stockpiled tents from regional warehouses to the flood‑affected villages within 24 hours.
Deploy QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, ARMVs and heli‑ambulances to the affected area.
Provide on‑site triage, resuscitation, and medical evacuation according to SOPs.
Prepare and dispatch medical kits containing IV fluids, ventilators, oxygen, dressing materials, tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, vaccines, anti‑snake venom and anti‑diarrhoea drugs.
Utilize identified large‑scale medical stores to procure additional supplies as needed.
Activate community‑level search and rescue teams trained by NDRF institutes.
Coordinate with NDRF battalions to assist state and district authorities in rescue operations.

final_json.report: The flood in Dadu requires immediate provision of water, food, shelter, medical help, medical products, and search and rescue operations. Public health guidelines call for safe water supply and clean food distribution (floods.pdf p67). Shelter plans mandate rapid deployment of tents via pre‑stockpiled supplies (ndmp-2019.pdf p313). Medical response includes QRMTs, mobile hospitals and a full complement of medical kits (a.pdf p63; floods.pdf p66). Search and rescue will be carried out by community teams and NDRF battalions (landslidessnowavalanches.pdf p125; floods.pdf p90). All required resources have sufficient evidential support; no evidence gaps were identified.

Conduct triage, resuscitation, and medical evacuation according to established SOPs.
Prepare medical kits containing IV fluid, ventilators, oxygen, dressing materials, tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, vaccines, anti‑snake venom, and anti‑diarrhoea drugs.
Identify large‑scale medical stores for procurement and distribute kits to health facilities.
Mobilize community‑level search and rescue teams trained by NDRF institutes.
Coordinate SAR operations with district authorities and ensure rapid deployment of teams.
Provide necessary equipment and maintain clear hand‑over procedures for subsequent rescue missions.

final_json.report: In Dadu, flood impacts have created urgent needs for water, food, shelter, medical assistance, medical supplies, and search‑and‑rescue operations. Public health authorities will ensure safe water and clean food distribution (water, food). Shelter response will be activated through pre‑identified suppliers and stocked materials (shelter). Medical help will be delivered via QRMTs, mobile hospitals, ARMVs, and heli‑ambulances with full triage and evacuation capabilities (medical_help). Essential medical products will be assembled into kits and sourced from large‑scale stores (medical_products). Search and rescue will rely on community teams trained by NDRF and coordinated with local agencies (search_and_rescue). All actions are based on the retrieved guidance documents; no evidence gaps were identified for the listed resources.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

provided after an earthquake will be done by a

Shelter response calls for pre‑planned supplier MOUs and stockpiled tents (ndmp-2019.pdf p313; landslidessnowavalanches.pdf p164). Emergency medical response assets (QRMTs, mobile hospitals, ARMVs, heli‑ambulances) are to be activated (a.pdf p63, p53). Medical product kits with IV fluids, antibiotics, vaccines, etc., are specified for flood casualties (floods.pdf p66, p67). All required resources have sufficient evidential support; no evidence gaps were identified.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

final_json.scenario: Help please, we need help at Christ-Roi street, Impasse Cedor. We need food, water, medical care and tents because there are two newborn babies in the.

instructions: Activate the public health response team to ensure safe water supply for the affected population.
Deploy water distribution points at Christ-Roi street, Impasse Cedor, using pre‑positioned water tanks or bottled water.
Coordinate with local agencies to monitor water quality and provide purification tablets if needed.
Utilize existing MOUs with food suppliers to procure family packs of essential food provisions.
Prioritize distribution of infant and small‑child nutrition packs for the newborns.
Set up food distribution centers at the incident site and ensure clean food handling as per public health guidelines.
Activate shelter suppliers identified in the DM plan to provide tents and tarpaulins within 24 hours.
Deploy stocked tents and temporary shelter materials from regional warehouses to the location.
Establish a temporary relief camp at Christ-Roi street with basic amenities for the affected families.
Mobilize QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, and ARMVs to the incident site for immediate medical response.
Provide dressing material, splints, portable X‑ray machines, and life‑saving drugs as outlined in the emergency medical SOPs.
Conduct triage, resuscitation, and arrange medical evacuation for any critical patients, especially the newborns.

final_json.report: The incident at Christ-Roi street, Impasse Cedor requires urgent delivery of water, food, shelter, and medical assistance for civilians including two newborns. Public health authorities will ensure safe water supply (floods.pdf p67) and food distribution (ndmp-2019.pdf p312; floods.pdf p67). Shelter operations will be activated using pre‑planned supplier agreements and stocked tents (ndmp-2019.pdf p313; landslidessnowavalanches.pdf p164). Medical response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, and ARMVs with full emergency medical equipment (a.pdf p63; a.pdf p53). All resources are confirmed as required and actionable based on the retrieved evidence.

instructions: Activate public health response teams to ensure safe water supply as mandated for flood aftermath.
Coordinate with local agencies and NGOs to set up water distribution points near Christ-Roi street.
Monitor water quality and provide treated water to affected families, especially newborns.
Mobilize food supply chains per MOU with suppliers to deliver family packs of essential food provisions.
Prioritize infant and small‑child nutrition supplies and lactating‑mother counseling kits.
Establish safe food distribution sites alongside water points, ensuring cleanliness and proper storage.
Identify shelter suppliers and activate MoUs for rapid provision of tents and tarpaulins within 24 hours.
Deploy stocked tents and temporary shelter materials from regional warehouses to Christ‑Roi street.
Set up a relief camp with basic amenities following IRS guidelines for relief camps.
Dispatch QRMTs, mobile field hospitals, ARMVs and heli‑ambulances to the incident site immediately.
Provide on‑site triage, resuscitation, and medical evacuation for victims requiring hospitalization.
Ensure availability of doctors, paramedical staff, and life‑saving equipment as outlined in emergency medical SOPs.
Prepare medical kits containing IV fluids, ventilators, oxygen, dressing materials, tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, vaccines, anti‑snake venom and anti‑diarrhoea drugs.
Utilize identified large‑scale medical stores to procure the listed supplies quickly.
Distribute medical products to the field hospitals and QRMT teams supporting the affected area.

Query evidence confirms the need for safe water, clean food, temporary shelters, and emergency medical response. All required resources have sufficient supporting documentation. Water distribution, food provision, rapid shelter deployment, dispatch of QRMTs/mobile field hospitals, and provisioning of comprehensive medical kits are being coordinated per the cited guidelines. No evidence gaps were identified.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which

8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

provided after an earthquake will be done by a

used as feedback for future improvement of the

and the requirement of blood and its components

Maintain a log of water quantities received, distributed, and remaining stock for accountability.
Coordinate with local health authorities to monitor dehydration cases and adjust water supply as needed.

No evidence gaps were found for the water resource.

7.6 Medical Preparedness and 
Response
7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical

operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.

equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an

7.6 Medical Preparedness and 
Response
7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

7.6.1 Preparedness
7.6.1.1 City hospitals should be adequately 
prepared to handle cases of flood-affected 
disasters and medicines for monsoon disasters.
7.6.1.2 In the event of an urban flood disaster, 
death could be due to drowning, injuries sustained 
due to damage to infrastructure like wall collapse, 
etc. Water borne diseases could immediately affect 
the people as a skin disease and vomitting. These 
incidences will also lead to outbreak of epidemics 
and skin diseases due to wading in flood waters 
and infection due to water borne diseases, such 
as dengue and malaria. Leptospirosis can be a 
serious threat, as people wading through water 
may get affected. Hospitals should have stocks 
of antibiotics and be in a position to requisition 
them at short notices. 
7.6.1.3 Diseases like malaria and dengue 
spread, if adequate sanitation and disinfection 
was not carried out. Cholera is also a possibility, 
because of the conditions that may be conducive 
for it. The important drugs are chlorine tablets.
7.6.1.4 The supply of safe and sufficient 
drinking water needs to be ensured. Protecting 
existing water sources from contamination, 
adding chlorine tablets in water for residual 
disinfection and provision of latrines and 
proper waste disposal to avoid contamination 
through flies and other insects, are important 
steps required immediately in the aftermath 
of an urban flood. Vector control is done by 
spraying of shelters with residual insecticides. 
Provision of insecticide-treated mosquito-nets 
and larviciding are recommended. Immunisation 
needs to be carried out in susceptible individuals 
to prevent diseases. Necessary arrangements 
should also be made to dispose off animal 
carcasses.
Local scale emergency medical response 
systems will be established to deal 
with medical preparedness, emergency 
treatment, mortuary facilities and disposal 
of bodies and carcasses, public health 
issues including trauma and control of 
epidemics.

8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.

equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.

If you are in an area at risk from
tsunamis
• You should find out if your home,
school, workplace, or other frequently
visited locations are in tsunami hazard
areas.
• Know the height of your street above
sea level and the distance of your
street from the coast or other high-
risk waters. (Local administration may

Evacuation orders may be based on
these numbers. Also find out the
height above sea level and the
distance from the coast of outbuildings
that house animals, as well as pastures
or corrals.
• Plan evacuation routes from your
home, school, workplace, or any other
place you could be where tsunamis
present a risk.
If possible, pick areas (30 meters)
above sea level or go as far as 3
kilometres inland, away from the
coastline. If you cannot get this high
or far, go as high or far as you can.
Every meter inland or upward may
make a difference. You should be able
to reach your safe location on foot
within 15 minutes. After a disaster,
roads may become blocked or
unusable. Be prepared to evacuate by
foot if necessary. Footpaths normally
lead uphill and inland, while many roads
parallel coastlines. Follow posted
tsunami evacuation routes; these will
lead to safety. Local emergency
management officials can advise you
on the best route to safety and likely
shelter locations.
• If your children's school is in an
identified inundation zone, find out
what the school evacuation plan is.
Find out if the plan requires you to pick
your children up from school or from
another location. Telephone lines
during a tsunami watch or warning may
be overloaded and routes to and from
schools may be jammed.
• Practice your evacuation routes.
Familiarity may save your life. Be able
to follow your escape route at night
and during inclement weather.
Practicing your plan makes the
appropriate response more of a
reaction, requiring less thinking during
an actual emergency situation.
• Use a Weather Radio or stay tuned to
a local radio or television station to
keep informed of local watches and
warnings.

lifelines and public safety, as well as individual 
buildings) or as a single, isolated event that affects 
a small geographic area, such as a highway or 
residential structures.

No evidence gaps were identified for the food resource.

No concrete guidance on water provision was found in the retrieved documents, resulting in an evidence gap for water. may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.

operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.

doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.

provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the

Emergency Medical Response
8.10.1  Prompt and efficient emergency medical
response will be provided by QRMTs, mobile field
hospitals, ARMVs and heli-ambulances. They will
be activated to reach the earthquake affected areas
immediately, along with dressing material, splints,
portable X-ray machines, mobile operation theatres,
resuscitation equipment and life-saving drugs, etc.
Resuscitation, triage and medical evacuation of
victims who require hospitalisation will be done in
accordance with SOPs. A large number of victims
may suffer from psycho-social trauma, for which
appropriate counselling will be provided.
8.10.2  The emergency medical plan will be
operationalised immediately on receiving
information from the earthquake affected areas.
Hospitals in the affected areas will create a surge
capacity for the required number of beds by
discharging non-critical patients and mobilise
doctors and support staff, additional orthopaedic
equipment and supplies at short notice. The
emergency medical plan will identify the
requirement of enhanced manpower, medical stores
and the requirement of blood and its components
for various levels of earthquakes. After an
earthquake, information centres will be set up to
provide medical response information to the public,
relatives of victims and media. The designated
hospitals will also identify the surgical teams that
can be deployed in the field at short notice and
arrange for their transport, medical equipment and
supplies. State governments will coordinate with
the hospitals, both government and private, in order
to facilitate effective and adequate hospital
response after earthquakes.
8.10.3  Documentation of medical response
provided after an earthquake will be done by a
medical administrator. This documentation will be
used as feedback for future improvement of the
response strategies.
Schedule for Response Activities
8.11.1  All the response activities outlined above
require detailed planning and comprehensive
mobilisation of manpower. The schedule given in
Table 10 (Pg 42) is considered reasonable at this
juncture; all activities will be institutionalised by and
continued beyond December 2008.

Flood Response
An effective and prompt response to floods 
is very important for minimising the loss of lives 
and properties and providing immediate relief 
to the affected people. The role of communities 
and NGOs is vital in search, rescue and relief 
operations. Immediate medical assistance to 
the affected people and steps for prevention of 
outbreak of epidemics after the floods are essential 
components of flood response. As per provisions of 
the DM Act, 2005, the GOI has constituted National 
Disaster Response Force (NDRF) for the purpose of 
specialised response to disasters. Over and above 
this, a mechanism for coordinated approach and 
efforts are required for effective response. All these 
aspects have been covered in the eighth chapter 
titled ‘Flood Response’.

Coordinate with central and state ministries to arrange transport of food grains to disaster‑affected areas.

Utilize FCI storage facilities to stage required quantities before distribution.

Prepare medical kits containing IV fluid, ventilators, oxygen, dressing materials, tetanus toxoid, antibiotics, vaccines, anti‑snake venom, and anti‑diarrhoea drugs.
Identify and activate large‑scale medical stores for procurement of the listed items.
Ensure trained medical and paramedical staff are on standby to distribute and administer the supplies.
Stock additional blood and IV fluid for transfusion and equip casualty rooms with resuscitation equipment (suction apparatus, airway devices, pulse oximeter, defibrillator).

All three resource categories have sufficient source material; no evidence gaps were identified.

8.9.1  Specialised heavy earthmoving equipment
and search and rescue equipment are required
immediately following an earthquake to clear debris
and to carry out search and rescue of trapped
people from collapsed structures. State
governments will compile a list of such equipment
and identify suppliers of such specialised

their mobilisation and deployment in the event of

resource inventory of  information on emergency
equipment and response personnel available in
every district, will be revised and updated frequently.

whose houses have been damaged by an

systems, transport and communication systems,
and medical supplies. The DM plans at the state
and district levels will address this issue in detail.
